extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of political theory, constitutional design, and history (readers of political-philosophical critique)
extracted.subtask_description: Assessing the strengths, weaknesses, and anti-corruption properties of different constitutional forms (aristocratic, democratic, mixed) using historical examples and institutional criteria. The page argues with examples from Roman history about checks, succession, and the social origins of public virtue.

rubrics_metrics.name: Checks and balances (three orders equal and independent)
rubrics_metrics.description: To control the tendency of concentrated power to corruption, three orders, equal and independent of each other, are contended for in the legislature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text: 'While power was in the hands of one, the few, or the many, has an impetuous propensity to corruption; and it is to control this tendency that three orders, equal and independent of each other, are contended for in the legislature.' Use institutional separation (multiple independent orders) as a primary safeguard against corruption.

rubrics_metrics.name: Presence and enforceability of term limits / rotation (succession)
rubrics_metrics.description: Regular succession and rotation in office (e.g., annually elective governors, senators, and representatives) is proposed as a preservative against corruption, but its efficacy is uncertain.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The United States example: making governors and legislatures annually elective 'have therefore a clear claim to his congratulations.' Yet the author warns the experiment is 'problematical' — succession might prevent or enable corruption; elections and succession must be guarded and monitored, and remedies prepared if corruption appears.

rubrics_metrics.name: Safeguards in electoral systems against corruption
rubrics_metrics.description: Elections of governors and senators must be adequately guarded to give reasonable hope against corruption.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text: 'The elections of governors and senators are so guarded, that there is room to hope; but, if we recollect the experience of past ages and other nations, there are grounds to fear.' Practical evaluation should consider how well election rules, franchise design, and oversight limit corrupting influences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Enforcement of laws versus rule by men
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether laws govern or are dispensed with by influential persons is a crucial criterion; a constitution where laws can be easily broken by those in power fails as a check.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Fabius asked 'Why laws were made, if they were to be broken or dispensed with by those who made them; and declared that the laws governed no longer, but were governed by men.' Evaluate the legal culture and institutional capacity to enforce rules against elite manipulation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Representative institutions must be checked to avoid crowning demagogues
rubrics_metrics.description: An unchecked people (or unchecked representative chamber) can elevate a popular benefactor to monarchical power; therefore representative bodies need checks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Spurius Melius used largesse to become popular and might have been made king had the senate not acted. The criterion: assess vulnerability of populace/representative bodies to demagogues who leverage philanthropy or popularity to seize power.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriateness of historical examples (representativeness)
rubrics_metrics.description: Historical examples used to justify constitutional claims must be representative of general conditions, not exceptional aristocratic cases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author criticises Nedham for quoting virtues 'which grew up only in a few aristocratical families' to prove the excellence of an unbalanced government. Guidance: avoid generalizing from elite exceptions; match example circumstances to the polity being designed or evaluated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prevalence and social basis of public virtue (frugality/disinterestedness)
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether civic virtues like frugality and disinterestedness are widespread or confined to a few aristocratic families affects how well a constitution will produce public-spirited leaders.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text argues such 'severe frugality' and 'perfect disinterestedness' are 'confined to a very few individuals or families' in aristocratic regimes and disappear under democracies except in crisis. Evaluate social incentives and whether virtue is systemic or exceptional.

rubrics_metrics.name: Standing authority concentration and corruption risk
rubrics_metrics.description: A standing authority concentrated in the hands of one, a few, or the many has an impetuous propensity to corruption.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this as a heuristic: concentrated, long-term authority increases corruption risk; institutional design should limit permanence and concentration of power via rotation or countervailing institutions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Whether institutions produce capable crisis leaders
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess whether the constitutional arrangement can produce or select capable, severe characters needed in times of danger (even if unpopular).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples (Curius, Camillus) show aristocratic selection sometimes yields capable commanders chosen for ability not popularity. Consider trade-offs: systems that favor able crisis leaders may also empower aristocratic pride and opposition to popular demands.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance between popular choice and aristocratic control (mutual checks on avarice)
rubrics_metrics.description: A functioning balance between elites and the people checks mutual excesses (e.g., avarice, plunder, bribery).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text: 'the senate and people were at this time checks on each other's avarice.' Evaluate how institutional interplay (electoral rights, senate powers, tribunes, etc.) constrains predatory behaviour on both sides.

rubrics_metrics.name: Policy for disposition of public spoils and public wealth
rubrics_metrics.description: Rules about whether plunder/presents are deposited in the public treasury or distributed to individuals affect stability and public sentiment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: debate over Veii's spoils — giving to citizens might cause sedition and complaints; appropriating to treasury might ease taxes. Evaluate fiscal rules governing seized wealth and public goods for their political consequences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Incentive structure for holding office (poverty vs. profit)
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess whether the office-holding rules and social-economic structures force those ambitious for magistracy to be poor/disinterested or allow enrichment via office.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In Rome, patricians who wanted magisterial office were 'obliged to be poor' because enriching routes were closed; this check produced certain virtues. Examine whether modern institutional incentives encourage public service or self-enrichment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Risk that succession/rotation itself may introduce corruption
rubrics_metrics.description: The practice of frequent succession or rotation can be either a preservative against corruption or an inlet to it; its net effect depends on enforcement and surrounding institutions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text is ambivalent: annual elections 'have therefore a clear claim' to praise but 'it is still problematical whether this succession will be the grand preservative against corruption, or the grand inlet to it.' Evaluate succession in context and prepare remedies if corruption appears.
